faqs.question: How long should a propose message in Hindi be?
faqs.answer: 25 to 40 words, sent as one message. That fits a single chat bubble and can be read in the few seconds between her seeing the notification and deciding how to feel. Anything longer is usually a sign you are explaining rather than asking.

faqs.question: Should I write it in Devanagari or in Roman Hindi?
faqs.answer: Whichever script she uses when she writes to you. Personal writing on social platforms skews heavily Roman — one 2014 study found 3,168 Roman-script posts against 73 Devanagari ones on a single celebrity Facebook page — while institutional pages stay in Devanagari. Sending polished Devanagari to someone who only ever types Roman reads as copied from a website.

faqs.question: Is it okay to propose in Hinglish?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most people under 30 it is the honest choice. Hinglish is Hindi in Roman script with ordinary English borrowings left in, and if that is already how the two of you write to each other, switching to formal Devanagari for one message draws attention to the switch rather than to the message.

faqs.question: Should I use tum or aap when proposing?
faqs.answer: तुम if you already talk daily and are of similar age; आप if there is respectful distance, such as a family introduction or someone you have never addressed informally. तू is either very intimate or rude depending on region and relationship, so do not use it for the first time in a proposal.

faqs.question: Can I just copy a propose shayari and send it?
faqs.answer: You can, but it will read as a forward. A shayari is a quotable line written for anyone; a message is written to one named person and usually contains a detail only the two of you know. If you do use a couplet, put it after your own sentence, not instead of it.

faqs.question: What should the first line say?
faqs.answer: Her name, plus the fact that something is coming — for example नेहा, एक बात कहनी है. A lock-screen preview shows only about 40 to 50 characters, so that is all she sees before deciding whether to open it, and it should contain nothing she would mind someone else glimpsing.

faqs.question: Is it better to send one message or several?
faqs.answer: One. Three messages mean three notifications, and the preview only ever shows the first, so the rest land after she has already started reacting. If your message will not fit one bubble, it is too long.

faqs.question: How do I end it so she can actually reply?
faqs.answer: End on a question she can answer in one word, such as क्या तुम मेरे बारे में भी ऐसा सोचती हो? A bare declaration leaves her to invent a reply format, which is where people freeze. If you do not want an answer immediately, say that explicitly: जवाब अभी नहीं चाहिए.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a propose message and a Propose Day wish in Hindi?
faqs.answer: A wish is a greeting, often sent to people you are not proposing to, and it works as a broadcast. A message is one piece of text sent to one person you are actually asking, which is why it needs her name, a real detail and a question at the end.

faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027?
faqs.answer: Monday 8 February 2027 — the second day of Valentine week, not the first. Rose Day falls on Sunday 7 February and Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February 2027. Because 8 February 2027 is a working Monday, the usable window is narrower than it was in 2026, when Propose Day fell on a Sunday.

faqs.question: Do I need a page, or is a plain text message enough?
faqs.answer: For a short message to someone you already know, plain text usually wins, and a page adds a step she has to take while deciding what to feel. A page earns its place when the message is the marriage question, or when distance means you cannot say it in person.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Message in Hindi: What to Type and Which Script

A propose message in Hindi works best as **one message, 25 to 40 words, addressed to her by name, written in the script she replies in, ending in a question she can answer in one word.** That is the answer; the rest is detail.

Two numbers shape it. Platform-wide across SubhSandesh's 4,567 personalised pages and 16 page types, 48.9% of views land on a phone (25,167 of 51,504) — so what she sees first is a notification preview, not your message. And sampled on our "I love you" pages (`/love-gf`, n=1,138), the median first-save-to-last-edit gap is 6.4 hours: people rewrite this all day before sending.

Below: five complete messages in Devanagari with Roman transliteration and English meaning, how to choose between scripts, the register trap that makes a message read like a film line, and when a plain message beats any page.

## What a propose message in Hindi has to do that a shayari does not

A shayari is a quotable line. A wish is a greeting sent to many. A **message** is one piece of text, typed into one chat box, sent to one named person, today.

That imposes constraints the quote lists never mention: her name in it, a length that fits one bubble, an ending she can answer without composing a speech of her own.

The pages ranking here are fragment lists — "100+", "360+", "700+" couplets, almost all Devanagari-only, none transliterated.

## Devanagari or Roman: pick the script she types in, not the one she reads

Most of this audience reads Devanagari comfortably and types in Roman. In a Microsoft Research Lab India study of English-Hindi code-mixing on Facebook, presented at the [2014 Workshop on Computational Approaches to Code Switching](https://aclanthology.org/W14-3914/), Amitabh Bachchan's page carried 3,168 posts in Roman script against 73 in Devanagari. The exception: on BBC Hindi News, Devanagari led at word level, 5,225 to 4,265.

Institutional writing stays Devanagari; personal writing goes Roman. The 2016 EMNLP study of 430,000 Hindi-English tweets by [Rudra and colleagues](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1121/) puts it flatly: on social media Hindi is seldom written in Devanagari, appearing instead as loose Roman transliteration.

So: **read her last five messages to you.** She types Roman, send Roman. She types Devanagari, send Devanagari. Polished Devanagari sent to someone who only types Roman is the clearest signal that you copied it off a website.

Roman has one cost. There is no standard spelling for Hindi in Latin script: the AI4Bharat team behind the [Aksharantar transliteration dataset](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.4/) note that मैं alone appears as *main*, *mai*, *mein* or *mei*, overlapping with में ("in"). Google Research's 2025 paper on [informally romanized language identification](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.117/) measures the same gap: systems near 99% accurate on native-script Indian languages drop to just over 80% on romanised text. In a full sentence, context resolves it; in a single word it does not.

A 2024 *Computational Linguistics* paper on [transliterating romanised South Asian text](https://doaj.org/article/96736b6a07b7433bad2c256c600f4856) makes the point from the systems side: informal romanisation here is a whole-sentence problem, not a word-by-word one.

## Five propose messages in Hindi, with transliteration and meaning

Each runs 25–40 words. Replace **नेहा / Neha** with her name, and the memory in #2 with one of yours — that swap is the difference between a message and a forward.

### 1. The plain one, if you are unsure

> नेहा, एक बात बहुत दिनों से कहनी थी। मुझे तुम बहुत अच्छी लगती हो — और अब दोस्ती से आगे सोचने लगा हूँ। क्या तुम मेरे बारे में भी ऐसा सोचती हो?

*Neha, ek baat bahut dinon se kehni thi. Mujhe tum bahut achhi lagti ho — aur ab dosti se aage sochne laga hoon. Kya tum mere baare mein bhi aisa sochti ho?*

"Neha, there's something I've wanted to say for a long time. I like you a lot — and I've started thinking beyond friendship. Do you think about me that way too?"

### 2. The one with a real memory in it

> नेहा, तुम्हें याद है पिछले हफ़्ते तुमने बिना पूछे मेरे लिए चाय भेज दी थी? उसी दिन समझ आया कि तुम मेरी कितनी आदत बन चुकी हो। मैं तुमसे प्यार करता हूँ।

*Neha, tumhein yaad hai pichhle hafte tumne bina poochhe mere liye chai bhej di thi? Usi din samajh aaya ki tum meri kitni aadat ban chuki ho. Main tumse pyaar karta hoon.*

"Neha, remember last week when you sent me tea without my asking? That was the day I understood how much of a habit you've become. I love you."

### 3. The direct question

> नेहा, सीधा पूछ रहा हूँ — क्या तुम मेरे साथ रहना चाहोगी? हाँ या ना, दोनों ठीक हैं। बस सच बता देना।

*Neha, seedha poochh raha hoon — kya tum mere saath rehna chahogi? Haan ya na, dono theek hain. Bas sach bata dena.*

"Neha, I'm asking straight — do you want to be with me? Yes or no, both are fine. Just tell me the truth."

### 4. The आप version, for respectful distance

> नेहा जी, पिछले कुछ महीनों में आपसे बात करके बहुत अच्छा लगा है। मैं इस रिश्ते को आगे ले जाना चाहता हूँ। आप आराम से सोचिए, फिर बताइए।

*Neha ji, pichhle kuchh mahinon mein aapse baat karke bahut achha laga hai. Main is rishte ko aage le jaana chahta hoon. Aap aaraam se sochiye, phir bataiye.*

"Neha ji, these past few months, talking to you has been really good. I want to take this further. Take your time, then tell me."

### 5. The Hinglish one, typed the way you actually type

> Neha, ek baat kehni thi — bahut din se soch raha tha. Tum mujhe bahut achhi lagti ho. Kya hum ise aage le ja sakte hain?

"Neha, I've been meaning to say something. I like you a lot. Can we take this forward?" Hindi in Roman with ordinary English borrowings left in. If that is how you two already write, do not upgrade it into Devanagari for the occasion.

## तुम, आप or तू — and why film-dialogue Hindi fails in a chat box

Hindi has three second-person pronouns where English has one. **तुम is the default** between people of similar age who talk daily. **आप** creates respectful distance and suits a family introduction, or anyone you have never addressed informally. **तू** is either very intimate or rude depending on region and relationship; if you have never used it with her, a proposal is the wrong place to start.

The bigger trap is vocabulary. वजूद, इबादत, मुक़द्दर and हसीन belong to film songs and ghazals; typed by someone who has never said them aloud, they read as quotation — she hears the screenwriter, not you. Everyday spoken Hindi does the work instead: *अच्छी लगती हो*, *साथ रहना*, *सोच रहा था*, *बात करनी थी*.

Read your line aloud. If you would be embarrassed saying it to her face, it lands worse in text, where she can reread it.

## The first line, the message count, and the ending

**The first line is the only line she sees before opening it.** A lock-screen preview shows roughly 40–50 characters. Put her name and the fact that something is coming — "नेहा, एक बात कहनी है" — nothing she would mind a flatmate seeing.

**Send one message, not three.** Three messages are three notifications, and the preview shows only the first; the rest arrive after she has started reacting. If it will not fit one bubble, it is too long.

**End with something answerable in one word.** "क्या तुम मेरे बारे में भी ऐसा सोचती हो?" takes हाँ. A declaration with no question leaves her inventing a reply format, which is where people stall. If you do not want an answer at once, say so: *"जवाब अभी नहीं चाहिए"*.

## Four ways to send it, compared

What each costs her, with SubhSandesh figures — all platform-wide, across 16 page types.

| What you send | Typical length | What it asks of her | SubhSandesh platform-wide data |
|---|---|---|---|
| One chat message | 25–40 words | Reads in seconds, replies in one word | 48.9% of page views are on a phone (25,167 of 51,504) |
| Three messages in a row | 60–90 words | Three notifications; preview shows only the first | — |
| Message plus a proposal page | 25 words plus a link | One tap, then a few minutes | 92.7% of started pages are published and shared (4,234 of 4,567) |
| Message plus a protected page | 25 words, link, password | Two steps before she reads anything | 39.9% of creators password-protect before sharing (1,822 of 4,567) |

If the marriage question is what you are asking, a page is where extra length belongs: put the story on a [proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) ending in a YES button, and keep the message to the line that gets her to open it. Asking her to be your girlfriend rather than your wife, the [romantic "I love you" page](/love-gf) fits better — our most-created template at 1,138 pages, 24.9% of everything built platform-wide. Asking again after a fight or a no, an [apology page](/apology-dashboard) does it better.

## When a plain message beats any page, including ours

For a short, well-judged message to someone you already know, a plain chat message usually wins. We would rather say that than sell you a link.

A page is a production: it costs time, asks her to tap through to a browser, and turns a private sentence into something that looks made. Right trade-offs for a marriage proposal; wrong ones for "I've liked you for months and I'm finally saying it", where the production reads as a way of not saying it plainly. On an old phone a text always opens and a page sometimes does not — and if you will be sitting in front of her tonight, say it out loud.

A last note on that 6.4-hour median edit gap sampled on `/love-gf`: it measures how long people keep fiddling, not how good the result is. Past a point, rewriting is avoidance. Take one of the five, change the name and a detail, read it aloud, send it.

## Sources

- Bali, Sharma, Choudhury, Vyas, ["I am borrowing ya mixing?" English-Hindi Code Mixing in Facebook](https://aclanthology.org/W14-3914/), October 2014.
- Rudra et al., [Understanding Language Preference for Expression of Opinion and Sentiment](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1121/), EMNLP, November 2016.
- Madhani et al., [Aksharantar: Indic-language Transliteration Datasets and Models](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.4/), Findings of EMNLP, December 2023.
- Benton, Gutkin, Kirov, Roark, [Improving Informally Romanized Language Identification](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.117/), EMNLP, November 2025.
- Kirov et al., [Context-aware Transliteration of Romanized South Asian Languages](https://doaj.org/article/96736b6a07b7433bad2c256c600f4856), Computational Linguistics, July 2024 — abstract only; the publisher's full text returned an error to our fetch.
